ABSTRACT

ASSESSING THE IMPACT OF CLIMATE CHANGE ON DEGRADATION OF THE SUNDARBANS MANGROVE FOREST: AN ORATORY FROM LANDSAT IMAGE ANALYSIS

Journal: Environment & Ecosystem Science (EES)

Author: Md. Mustafizur Rahaman”, Shammi Akter Satu”, Abhijit Biswas, Abul Kalam Azad

This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License CC BY 4.0, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited

DOI: 10.26480/ees.01.2026.50.56

The Sundarbans is recognized as the world’s richest mangrove biodiversity hotspot, often referred to as the “lungs” of Bangladesh. Over the last few decades, this ecosystem has undergone considerable degradation, largely driven by climate change. Consequently, this study seeks to answer the question: “How is the degradation of the Sundarbans being influenced by climate change?” The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) was employed to delineate the extent of degradation between 1990 and 2022. NDVI values ranging from -1.0 to 1.0 were considered: positive values indicate the presence of vegetation, negative values. correspond to water bodies and values approaching zero represent bare land. Additionally, to assess the impact of climate change on mangrove degradation, trends in climatic variables, i.e., temperature, rainfall, and humidity, have been analyzed. The annual states of vegetation, water body, and bare land have been correlated with the respective mean temperature, rainfall, and humidity for each year. The results found that approximately 43.68 km² of mangrove area was lost between 1990 and 2022. Mangrove forests possess an inherent capacity for self-regeneration following destruction; however, frequent cyclones after 2007 have significantly hindered this recovery process, contributing to substantial vegetation loss. Furthermore, the mean temperature in January gradually decreases over this period, while the mean humidity and rainfall increase. This change has the potential to disturb mangrove regeneration. Correlational analysis of these climatic variables and state of degradation revealed a correlation coefficient of 0.464 for humidity, 0.312 for temperature, and -0.377 for rainfall. Although these values suggest a negative impact on mangrove vegetation regrowth, they do not demonstrate a strong or significant correlation. Hence, climate change is accelerating the degradation of mangrove forests by increasing the frequency of cyclones, while changing trends in climatic variables further intensify the associated threats.
